concepts.title: Make agents prove outcomes, not narrate success
paragraphs: Hallie recommends converting intent into intermediate checks and enforcing essential verification in hooks and CI, rather than trusting a persuasive completion message. At Duolingo, Agrawal describes restricting generated test changes, automated review and human approval; coverage gains were reported by the team and do not by themselves prove fewer defects. Robinhood combines deterministic checks with an agent looking for contextual risks beyond those checks, while retaining people for sensitive or uncertain decisions.

225,000 Lines of Tests, Written and Merged by Agents - Kush Agrawal, Duolingo

concepts.title: Evaluate the evaluator—and hold out real variations
paragraphs: LinkedIn’s Gandhi and Guo found that their judge confused some weak outputs and that a reflection system could misattribute errors; they improved rubrics with human review before using feedback to optimize prompts. Ramp’s Stevens describes replayable bookkeeping worlds and skill ablations, while Kanazawa found his agent-written rubric had overfit one lecture and needed testing on other videos. These are different evaluation settings, but each shows why a good-looking score or a single successful example is not enough.

videos.title: An Agent That Fixes Its Own Mistakes - Saloni Gandhi & Ziwei Guo, LinkedIn
How Ramp Tests Its AI Bookkeeping Agent Before Customers Do - Ryan Stevens, Ramp
I Let Agents Refactor My Codebase for 3 Weeks. Then I Read the Code. — Keiji Kanazawa, Microsoft

concepts.title: Isolation protects execution, not permission to cause harm
paragraphs: Hallie distinguishes deny rules from sandboxing: an approved command can still run child code, and her described shell sandbox does not cover every agent component. A disposable machine also cannot undo a pushed commit or a sent message; Ivanda similarly warns that tools invoked outside an embedded runtime can retain host privileges, although his separate-machine recommendation comes from a sandbox vendor. Ben Chaim’s skill-testing work adds that dynamic tests only observe the routes exercised, so a clean run is not proof of safety.

videos.title: Rethinking Claude Code Best Practices — Lydia Hallie, Anthropic
The One Thing Every AI Agent Framework Agrees On - Mislav Ivanda, Daytona
You Can't Tell What an Agent Skill Will Do by Reading It - Roey Ben Chaim, Zenity

concepts.title: Treat delegation as a distributed system with uncertain effects
paragraphs: Konda argues that a timeout after a tool call does not establish whether the action happened: track evidence and side effects, bind approval to the action, and read back state before retrying. The UndoBench speakers make the related distinction between safe retry, restoration and compensation, proposing pre-state witnesses and tested recovery plans. These are proposed engineering approaches and benchmark findings, not guarantees that every external action can be reversed.

videos.title: Your Sub-Agents Are a Distributed System. Treat Them Like One. - Girish Konda, Microsoft
Your Coding Agent Can't Undo Its Own Mistakes - Tanmay Sah & Dolly Sah

concepts.title: More parallel agents move the bottleneck to shared capacity and merge
paragraphs: Harvey’s Wang reports that duplicate alerts spawned redundant work and that a large burst of CLI tasks blocked colleagues, motivating deduplication and a fair launch queue; he says merge scaling remains unsolved. Uber’s speakers describe a different tradeoff: relaxing some pre-merge conflict checks for throughput, then maintaining a separately validated main pointer. That improves reported throughput at the cost of allowing some untested combinations onto raw main, with the reliability cost unquantified in the talk.

videos.title: The Agents Were Fine. Everything Around Them Broke. - Joey Wang, Harvey
AI Writes Code Faster Than Uber Can Merge It - Preetam Dwivedi & Manjari Akella, Uber

concepts.title: Preserve corrections as testable context, not an ever-growing prompt
paragraphs: Linear’s Moor describes enriching issues with prior decisions and extracting lessons from feedback and reverts, while warning against enormous instruction files. Douglas suggests capturing agent sessions and review corrections, then starting with reusable skills and evaluations rather than assuming post-training is necessary. Petrov adds a way to test whether a skill contributes: compare defined tasks with and without it, and keep deletions only if task performance survives; what a model already knows varies with the model and the grading standard.

videos.title: What Your Coding Agent Can't See in the Code - Tom Moor, Linear
Every Correction You Give Your Agent Is Data - Brian Douglas, Paper Compute
Your SKILL.md Is 70% Stuff the Model Already Knows - Nikolay Petrov, Intel

concepts.title: Trace financial conclusions to assumptions and source versions
paragraphs: In the Costco forecasting exercise, the Together AI speakers found an unsupported membership assumption and an incorrect geographic scope whose errors partly cancelled, making a close forecast misleading. Fieldguide’s Veeraragavan argues that consequential audit conclusions also need stable evidence identity and version, recorded decision steps, and protection for work a human has already reviewed. His reconciliation example is fictional, and these controls are an assurance design—not proof of regulatory compliance.

videos.title: Right Answer, Wrong Reasons: AI Forecasts Costco - Hassan El Mghari & Omar El Mghari, Together AI
Your Financial Agent Needs to Show Its Work - Anirudh Veeraragavan, Fieldguide

concepts.title: Catch ambiguity before an agent faithfully builds the wrong thing
paragraphs: AWS’s Kotyal proposes translating requirements into formal constraints to expose conflicts, gaps and alternative interpretations before implementation. A solver checks the constraints it receives, not whether the translation reflects the owner’s intent, so unresolved interpretations still need domain judgment. In a separate workshop, Monzo’s presenters similarly put clarification and explicit assumptions ahead of reusable calculations; their example is illustrative, not a production benchmark.

Stop Chatting With Spreadsheets — Francesco Galletta & Felippe Felisola Caso, Monzo
Stop Shipping LLM Settings That Only Win on Paper - Rohan Pandey & Balaji Varadarajan, DigitalOcean
videos.overview: This demonstration presents an agent that searches for better LLM-serving configurations using Optuna and Bayesian optimization. It shows the workload definitions, inputs, and output artifacts, then reports performance improvements from two earlier tuning runs without supplying enough benchmark detail to establish generalizable gains.
key_points: The agent automates repeated serving-configuration experiments, replacing manual parameter exploration with an Optuna search loop guided by Bayesian optimization.
Each trial evaluates a candidate recipe, assigns a score, and uses the result to guide subsequent configurations rather than exhaustively testing every combination.
The demonstrated workload mix includes short chat, long chat, retrieval-augmented generation, and batch classification, each with configurable input and output token lengths.
The tuning script takes a study name, starting YAML recipe, hardware description, and trial budget; runs are described as taking hours.
The GPT-OSS report is said to improve generated-token performance by 17.5% relative to its initial configuration, with scoring described in terms of goodput.
A separate DeepSeek R1 distill run reportedly doubled token throughput and reduced inter-token latency by almost half across nine trials.
The outputs are an HTML trial report and an optimized YAML recipe, allowing both inspection of the search and reuse of its selected configuration.
summary: The demo targets the practical work of finding a suitable serving recipe for a model on particular hardware. Instead of having an engineer repeatedly change settings and benchmark them manually, an optimization agent conducts the experiments in the background. The speaker describes Bayesian optimization as the search strategy and Optuna as the tool managing trials, collecting scores, and proposing subsequent candidates. The intended benefit is faster discovery through a guided search rather than exhaustive parameter enumeration.

The starting configuration includes four workload regimes: short chat, long chat, retrieval-augmented generation, and batch classification. Each has input- and output-token lengths that can be adjusted to represent the intended traffic. After downloading model weights to a droplet and activating an environment, the operator runs tuner.py with a study name, initial YAML, hardware information, and trial budget. The illustrated command requests 24 trials, while the separate GPT-OSS results report covers 50; these are distinct examples, not a single documented execution.

Results are delivered as an HTML report identifying the best trial and a YAML file containing the selected recipe. For the GPT-OSS example, the speaker reports a 17.5% improvement over the initial configuration and describes goodput tokens as the scoring basis. A DeepSeek R1 distill example uses nine trials, with the final trial selected as best; reported token throughput doubles while inter-token latency falls by almost half. These are serving-performance claims, not evidence of improved answer quality. The demo establishes an inspectable tuning workflow, but does not provide the complete search space, hardware specifications, benchmark repetitions, or goodput acceptance criteria needed to reproduce or generalize the gains.

videos.title: Rethinking Claude Code Best Practices — Lydia Hallie, Anthropic
videos.overview: Lydia Hallie explains how coding-agent best practices change when developers supervise many long-running sessions instead of approving individual steps. Her central distinction is between capabilities entrusted to the model and safeguards enforced through permissions, isolation, verification hooks, and CI.
key_points: As models improve, instruction files should emphasize facts unavailable from the repository rather than redundant stack descriptions or emphatic reminders; Hallie says excessive steering can worsen results.

Automatic command approval is a probabilistic filter, not a security boundary. Hallie reports that a study blocked 89% of dangerous commands with auto mode, compared with roughly 14% caught by human approvers.
Explicit deny rules protect against prohibited tool calls, while an operating-system sandbox constrains what an approved command and its child processes can actually access.
A disposable cloud machine reduces exposure to local credentials and supports unattended execution, but commits, connector messages, and other external effects still require controls.
Define intermediate acceptance checks so plausible but undesirable implementations fail early; an authentication migration might otherwise preserve obsolete behavior or log everyone out.
Hooks and CI should enforce verification rather than merely requesting it in a prompt. Hallie specifically describes hook exit code 2 as the signal that sends the agent back to repair a failure.
Scale through independent review, risk-adjusted human approval, and an orchestrator that delegates implementation to separate sessions and rejects incomplete work.
summary: Hallie frames the shift to autonomous coding as a redistribution of responsibilities. Developers previously steered implementations, approved commands, inspected changes, and started each session themselves. In her account, stronger models now handle much of the steering, while automatic approval reduces interruptions. Consequently, repository instructions should retain hidden operational facts, such as an undocumented legacy dependency, rather than repeat information the agent can discover. She also describes an instruction-audit feature for identifying guidance that newer models no longer need.

Safety requires distinguishing permission to execute from constraints on execution. A deny rule can prevent a direct attempt to read a sensitive file, but an apparently harmless test command may execute compromised dependency code that accesses credentials indirectly. Sandboxing addresses that second problem by restricting filesystem and network access for commands and their descendants. Hallie notes that the shell sandbox does not encompass the agent's own file operations, MCP servers, or hooks, so it is not complete session isolation.

Cloud sessions provide a broader boundary: each receives a fresh repository copy on a separate machine, without unrelated local secrets, and can continue after the developer closes a laptop. Hallie describes restricted network access and network secrets that provide credentials without exposing them to the model. However, a disposable machine does not make its external actions disposable. Pushed commits and connector messages persist, so automatic approval and explicit restrictions remain necessary even in isolated environments.

Verification replaces the confidence formerly gained from watching every step. Hallie's authentication-migration example shows why an apparently reasonable implementation can still violate intent. Define intermediate pass/fail checks, request actual execution output, and enforce essential checks through hooks. She highlights the hook failure-code contract, then extends the pattern to CI, automatic repair, and independent agent review using fresh context. Human review should match change risk rather than disappear universally. Finally, an orchestrator can start implementation sessions, assess their results, and return unfinished work for correction. Her suggested experiment is one unusually large cloud task, backed by meaningful CI, followed by inspecting where human intervention remains necessary.

videos.title: Your Spec Has Bugs. Catch Them Before Your Agent Codes. - Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal, AWS
videos.overview: An AWS automated-reasoning project checks specifications for ambiguity, contradictions, and missing cases before a coding agent implements them. The proposed division of labor is deliberately limited: models translate requirements, solvers examine their logical relationships, and humans resolve questions of intended behavior.
key_points: Requirements can look sensible individually but conflict when combined, as when an inventory rule requires backorders while another rule prohibits them.
The pipeline first attempts language refinement, then translates requirements into SMT formulas and uses a satisfiability solver to check the resulting constraints.
Repeated translations are clustered by logical equivalence to expose materially different interpretations rather than treating one model-generated formalization as authoritative.
Ambiguity, conflict, and missing coverage require different responses: clarify intended meaning, reconcile incompatible rules, or supply an absent rule.
Formal analysis cannot recover implicit domain knowledge or establish that a specification expresses what its owner actually wants.
summary: The talk moves verification upstream from generated code to the requirements that guide its creation. Its opening example is an e-commerce specification containing incompatible instructions: an unavailable item should become a backorder, but another rule forbids backorders altogether. Each sentence appears reasonable in isolation; the defect emerges from their interaction. The speaker argues that reviewing wording alone is insufficient because a coding agent must also reconcile relationships across a rulebook.

The proposed analyzer uses a staged process. An LLM first tries to refine unclear language. Requirements are then expressed as SMT formulas so a satisfiability solver can examine the formalized constraints. Detected problems are fed back for reconsideration rather than silently passed downstream to implementation. This separates generating a plausible interpretation from checking its logical consequences, although it does not establish that the translation faithfully captures the user's intent.

To investigate translation uncertainty, the system asks for seven or ten translations and groups them by logical equivalence. Multiple equivalent formulations differ from genuinely different interpretations, so clustering helps identify where clarification is needed. The talk distinguishes vague operations, contradictory rules, and uncovered cases. Removing a record could mean permanent deletion or merely hiding retained data; contradictory backorder rules require reconciliation; an idle order without an applicable rule exposes a coverage gap. These examples show why the next step may be a targeted question rather than more autonomous coding.

The conclusion keeps the specification owner responsible for correctness. Humans possess domain knowledge that neither a language model nor a solver can assume, and the speaker describes evidence for agent-oriented formalization as still emerging. The system may accept an interpretation, request clarification, or abstain from implementing an unresolved requirement; LLM judges are also mentioned as a fallback. The practical lesson is not that formal methods eliminate requirements review, but that they can make it more focused by presenting explicit alternatives and conflicts before those uncertainties become code.

videos.title: Your SKILL.md Is 70% Stuff the Model Already Knows - Nikolay Petrov, Intel
videos.overview: Nikolay Petrov presents a method for measuring which parts of an agent skill add knowledge, repeat existing knowledge, fail to teach, or actively hurt performance. He treats that analysis as a guide for editing skills, while insisting that actual task evaluations must decide whether the edits preserve useful behavior.
key_points: Knowledge-providing skills and process-steering skills serve different purposes; information already known by a model can still be useful when the goal is repeatable behavior.
Establish a task-level baseline by comparing runs with and without the skill, tracking completion alongside token consumption and elapsed time.
Break a skill into atomic propositions or behavioral contracts, then generate question-and-answer probes for those items without leaking the answers in the questions.
Evaluate both conditions with a judge, preferably from another model family or a panel, while explicitly deciding whether tools and web access are available.
Classify each item into four outcomes: already known, made worse by the skill, newly learned with the skill, or still unanswered despite the skill.
Strict detail checks can reveal much less prior knowledge than broad conceptual checks; one reported comparison drops from approximately 70% to 22%.
Use novelty measurements to choose edits, not to certify them: removing apparently redundant content is beneficial only if downstream task evaluations still pass.
summary: Petrov distinguishes skills that teach unfamiliar information from skills that impose a repeatable process. His analysis focuses on the first category, without dismissing the usefulness of steering. He begins with task evaluations: run the same defined problems with and without a skill, then compare success, token use, and completion time. An illustrative improvement from three solved tasks to five shows how to measure added capability rather than relying on whether the instructions appear sensible.

To make optimization less arbitrary, he proposes decomposing a skill into atomic items inspired by fact-score methods. Items may express factual propositions or more specific behavioral contracts. Each receives an expected answer and a question designed not to reveal that answer. The target model answers with and without the skill; a separate judge, ideally from another model family or a panel, assesses correctness. Tool availability must also be controlled, since closed-book knowledge and knowledge recoverable through web access answer different practical questions.

The paired results produce four categories. Correct answers in both conditions suggest existing knowledge; failure without the skill followed by success with it indicates added knowledge. Success becoming failure identifies harmful instructions, while failure in both conditions suggests the material has not taught the concept effectively. Petrov describes visualizing these categories across the source text to guide edits. He also separates lenient conceptual judging from strict checks of exact keys, values, and procedures: one reported comparison moves from roughly 70% prior understanding to 22% when precise details are required.

The operational lesson is to preserve useful specificity while testing whether broad explanations can be shortened. Prior knowledge varies across skills and models, so a redundancy estimate is not universal and should be revisited as models change. Most importantly, novelty is only a diagnostic signal. Remove selected already-known material, rerun the original task evaluations, and keep the reduction only when performance is preserved. Petrov closes by placing this analysis within a broader context-evaluation framework covering skills, agent instructions, MCP tools, routing, and descriptions, but the supplied transcript does not reliably identify that framework by name.

videos.title: Pick Problems That Survive When AI Solves Coding - Ara Khan, Cline
videos.overview: Ara Khan uses an autonomous coding-harness improvement experiment to explain how AI systems can participate in improving their own operating stack. He connects that engineering pattern to a career-selection argument: choose problems that become more valuable as models improve, rather than problems a stronger model could simply erase.
key_points: The concrete self-improvement example changes an agent's harness through repeated evaluation and code edits; it is not evidence that the underlying model autonomously improved its weights or reached general intelligence.

Useful agent evaluation checks completed environmental outcomes, not merely plausible answers. Khan describes sandboxed tasks, independent grading, trajectory inspection, and checks against cheating or reward hacking.

A meta-agent can run evaluations, categorize failures, modify the harness, and repeat. Reported failure categories include repetitive loops, background processes running too long, and file-index problems.
Khan argues that optimization opportunities span the stack: evaluation, training data, post-training, inference kernels, networking, firmware, and interaction with physical devices.
Human corrections identify gaps at the current capability frontier. Turning those gaps into verifiable tasks creates targets for subsequent improvement.

His career advice distinguishes work that benefits from stronger models from work that stronger models can eliminate. He favors ambitious infrastructure, data, hardware, and other contributions to the improvement pipeline.
summary: Khan frames recursive self-improvement around three concerns: understanding frontier laboratories' direction, choosing a resilient engineering career, and avoiding an economy in which most gains accrue to model and hardware providers. His practical example is narrower than the speculative endpoint. A coding agent can alter the software harness surrounding another model, test whether those alterations help, and repeat. This improves the deployed system without necessarily changing model weights. He situates the example within a progression from conversational coding assistance to tool use, multi-agent interaction, and increasingly autonomous improvement loops, while presenting further acceleration as an expectation rather than an established outcome.

The engineering mechanism starts with evaluations that distinguish claiming completion from actually completing a task. Setting up an MCP integration, for example, can require research, configuration edits, software installation, database changes, and shell commands; a final success message proves little by itself. Khan describes Terminal-Bench runs using isolated parallel containers, followed by grading of outcomes and inspection of turns, tokens, latency, tool calls, and trajectories. Engineers then group failures and change the harness to address recurring causes. His proposed automation gives that diagnostic and editing work to a supervising agent. In the reported experiment, it identified looping behavior, overly persistent background processes, and file-index issues, then iteratively modified the harness and reran evaluations. He emphasizes that improvements should generalize across tasks rather than exploit the benchmark or overfit a single live problem.

The broader argument is that this feedback pattern is not confined to agent scaffolding. Khan cites purported AI-generated production-kernel optimizations and an agent-assisted kernel competition as examples of extending improvement into inference infrastructure. He reports serving-cost and generation-efficiency gains, but supplies no independently assessable evidence in the transcript. He also interprets everyday user corrections, such as fixing a database cache configuration or its TTL, as signals exposing the boundary of current capability. A hardware anecdote makes the loop tangible: a small camera, microphone, and speaker device responded slowly, so he connected it to a computer and used coding agents to run tests, locate latency, and experiment with firmware, tool calls, inference choices, and speech recognition. The important enabling condition is a measurable outcome against which successive changes can be judged.

Khan closes by turning this technical pattern into a filter for projects and careers. He worries that engineers building narrowly scoped applications may be creating work that the next model release makes unnecessary, while contributing little beyond relaying instructions to a coding assistant. His alternative is not simply to pursue harder problems: it is to seek endeavors that benefit from model progress without being solved by model scaling alone, ideally while helping produce further progress. He includes data pipelines, inference, post-training, hardware, networking, and community among possible directions. He also acknowledges a timing tradeoff: an ambitious project may become easier if one waits for a stronger model. His compressed timelines and advice to move toward the improvement loop remain personal strategic judgments, not demonstrated predictions about which businesses or careers will survive.

videos.title: Agents Made Code Free. Maintaining It Didn't Get Cheaper. - Dmitry Buykin, Maersk
videos.overview: Dmitry Buykin describes maintaining an agent-driven system whose business instructions span countries and processes, after a destructive rewrite failed to prevent complexity from returning. His alternative combines expert-readable rules, constrained runtime behavior, evidence-based verification, and weekly maintenance loops that do not depend on one exhausted architect.
key_points: Cheap code generation accelerated complexity growth; a large cleanup lost useful behavior and did not stop the system from becoming tangled again.
Business prose is an engineered part of the system, requiring explicit ownership, linting, task-based review, and consistency with executable behavior.
Repeated, stable execution paths can become workflow tools, while variable business judgments remain in expert-readable decision tables with human fallback.
Runtime control includes limiting model-visible facts, validating references to retained data, constraining writes, and journaling actions to prevent duplicate execution on retries.
Verification should use real-task replays, deliberately failing checks, preserved decision branches, and independent review rather than treating green dashboards as sufficient evidence.
Feedback ledgers, cross-slice investigations, usage evidence, and weekly cleanup distribute maintenance work while preserving legitimate country-specific differences.
summary: Buykin begins with a failed response to agent-generated complexity: a sweeping rewrite removed unused-looking tests and boilerplate, lost useful pieces, and still allowed the mess to grow back. His alternative is continuous maintenance below the volume of change people can meaningfully inspect. The system he describes spans 110 countries and approximately 10,000 instruction scenarios, organized into process-and-country slices. Changes normally stay within their slice. Because much of the system is prose, correctness requires business experts as well as developers; sentence mutations that barely affected tests exposed weak protection for those instructions.

The architecture separates stable execution from variable judgment. Repeated agent paths become workflow tools when behavior agrees across countries, and duplicated procedural instructions must then be removed to prevent agents repeating those steps. Experts own readable decision tables, code prepares facts and executes actions, and unmatched cases return to people. The boundary can move in either direction: unreadable expressions may leave code for prose. Context is also a control surface. Giving a model unnecessary pricing information prompted an invented pricing check, so the runtime supplies only relevant facts and retains larger records behind validated handles. Write controls and journaling address unsafe or repeated actions.

The operational bottleneck became the architect's attention. Buykin replaced personally relaying feedback with user-facing evaluation loops and ledgers connecting issues to root causes. Records distinguish historical events from current truth so subsequent sessions do not reason from stale assumptions. Isolated signals may warrant waiting, while repeated failures across slices trigger investigation of the shared concept. Agents search related slices, but apply fixes only where the failure is confirmed because market and legal differences can be intentional.

Verification becomes the limiting resource. Real-task replay is preferred evidence, new checks must fail deliberately before being trusted, and refactors must preserve decision branches. A branch with no supporting real task is labeled as lacking evidence rather than assumed covered. A second agent reviews against a checklist without the author's reasoning, while ledgers expose skipped batch work. Weekly cleanup then uses usage evidence to retire variants and their associated tests instead of preserving every historical option. Some gauges and further workflow composition remain planned. The closing warning is that the resulting system inherits the habits and biases of whoever repeatedly corrects it.

videos.title: 225,000 Lines of Tests, Written and Merged by Agents - Kush Agrawal, Duolingo
videos.overview: Kush Agrawal explains how Duolingo turned agent-generated unit tests into a managed production workflow rather than an unattended stream of pull requests. The reported result is more than 700 human-approved test PRs, with the largest coverage gains concentrated in the more testable MVVM portion of its iOS app.
key_points: Duolingo reports approximately 225,000 added test-code lines, overall coverage rising from 11% to 24%, and combined MVVM-layer coverage rising from 9% to 59%.
The reusable workflow is identify, write, verify, resolve, and iterate; Temporal orchestrates durable execution while S3 stores shared state and GitHub manages PRs.
File selection favors view models, repositories, and data sources, penalizes large files, and excludes UI code from this unit-test backfill.
PR lifecycle management bounds repair attempts, handles stale work, routes green PRs to source-code contributors, and pauses rejected files to avoid reviewer spam.
Quality controls combine deterministic file-scope restrictions, automated code review, a dedicated LLM judge, and mandatory human approval.
Moving agents from Linux to Mac runners enabled local build and lint checks, addressing an environmental limitation that prompts alone could not fix.
summary: Duolingo's iOS repository was approaching two million executable lines while AI tools broadened who could contribute. Agrawal frames verification, rather than code production, as the bottleneck. The team focused on the MVVM half of a mature, partially migrated codebase because it was easier to test than legacy code. Over eight months, it reports overall unit-test coverage increasing from 11% to 24% and combined MVVM-layer coverage from 9% to 59%, with every merged generated PR approved by a human.

The team first tested viability locally, using coverage reports to select files and agents to write tests and open PRs. Early batches achieved roughly half their proposed merges, but their main value was exposing failure modes. Agents mixed XCTest with Swift Testing, struggled to mock a concrete singleton, and produced concurrency or timing-related problems. Responses included clearer testing guidance, migration to a protocol-based dependency with lint enforcement, and better examples. Production orchestration then used Temporal workflows, shared S3 state, and GitHub integration. Selection favored view models, repositories, and data sources while deprioritizing large or legacy files and skipping UI code.

Generating PRs created a separate operational problem: getting them safely reviewed and merged. A recurring lifecycle workflow takes one action per eligible PR, closes conflicted or roughly three-week-old work, waits for running CI or active reviewers, and assigns green PRs using source-file contribution history. Deterministic pre-commit fixes avoid unnecessary agent calls; substantive failures trigger agent repairs capped at five attempts. Rejected files receive a 30-day cooldown. Engineers can also request tests for their own changes through a label-triggered workflow rather than waiting for scheduled backfills.

Quality required more than passing CI. Agents sometimes changed production code, weakened existing tests, or introduced long waits. The pipeline therefore restricts allowed file categories, resolves critical automated-review findings, and applies a specialized LLM judge before human review. Moving execution to Mac runners let agents build and lint locally instead of discovering errors through delayed CI. The resulting pipeline reportedly merged more than 700 PRs and added about 225,000 test-code lines. Agrawal closes by extending the workflow pattern to migrations and snapshot testing, while presenting classifier-based lifecycle decisions as a future experiment rather than a deployed result.

videos.title: Your Team's Agents Are All Shipping to the Same Code at Once - Patrick Debois, Tessl
videos.overview: Patrick Debois argues that parallel coding agents require a delivery system designed for concurrency, not merely more automated coding loops. He connects code coordination, semantic conflicts, human decision-making, and risk-based review into a proposed operating model for multiplayer software factories.
key_points: Agent-generated pull requests shift bottlenecks toward integration, repeated CI runs, human approvals, and maintenance of the factory itself; generating more changes does not automatically improve delivery throughput.

Coordinate work before implementation through task partitioning, ticket claims, and announcements of intended file changes, then isolate more than Git state when agents need independent execution environments.
Textually compatible changes can conflict in intent: changing invoice calculations to cents can silently break a report that still expects dollars even when both pull requests pass their own checks.
Shared conversations can turn requirements gathering into a collaborative planning process, including sales, support, and marketing without bypassing engineering practices.
Human attention should be reserved for well-framed decisions and exceptions, supported by contextual IDE handoffs, decision logs, small reviewable changes, and concrete verification evidence.
Review policy should reflect both failure likelihood and impact, using human scrutiny, gradual rollout, rollback, and restoration capabilities according to the change's risk.
A factory team analogous to a platform team would maintain shared skills, context, integrations, monitoring, and the delivery system's own reliability.
summary: Debois distinguishes a solo software factory, where one developer coordinates agents and remembers their decisions, from a multiplayer factory in which several people and agents share a codebase and task board. Traditional build-test-merge pipelines assume a largely serial progression. Increasing agent output exposes that assumption: pull requests accumulate, agents overwrite or reverse one another's changes, and each merge can trigger rebases and repeated testing elsewhere. The queue also includes agent-caused incidents and improvements to skills and execution loops, not just customer features. His proposed shift from continuous to concurrent delivery means treating simultaneous work as the normal operating condition rather than an exceptional integration problem.

The first intervention is better allocation and coordination. Divide work by subsystem or finer-grained code boundaries, have agents claim tickets, and publish their intended changes so overlap becomes visible before implementation. Worktrees help, but independent execution may also require separate context, pinned API versions, database snapshots, test data, and simulated external systems. When collisions occur, agents can wait, retry, requeue, or renegotiate the plan rather than blindly continue. Debois also separates line-level merge conflicts from semantic disagreement. His invoice example changes calculations from dollars to cents while another change updates reporting: the code can merge successfully while the combined behavior violates expectations. He proposes intent-aware checking and speculative merge trains that pretest compatibility so one troublesome candidate need not stall other ready changes.

The human side requires a shared coordination surface rather than several private prompting sessions. An agent participating in team chat can gather requirements from multiple people, ask clarifying questions, and turn the discussion into a shared execution plan. Non-engineers can then initiate or refine changes through the same pipeline, context, and engineering practices rather than produce disconnected prototypes. For work that needs rapid exploration, he cites a Helix ML approach that opens an IDE with the agent's exact working context, lets a human intervene, and hands execution back afterward. Bounded decision options and a shared decision ledger reduce repeated explanation while preserving who decided what. Change size must also reflect human review capacity, not just agent parallelism.

Debois rejects a universal answer to whether humans should stop reading generated code. Documentation changes and authentication changes have different consequences, so review intensity should follow risk. Better context, adversarial review, screenshots, videos, and test evidence can reduce uncertainty; gradual releases, fast rollback, and data restoration can reduce the cost of being wrong. High output also creates a communication problem: support and marketing need changes translated into their own operational language. He therefore anticipates a factory team that owns shared skills, context freshness, integrations, and monitoring. The closing extension is personal agents that answer questions or make delegated decisions on the board. He presents this as an emerging direction, explicitly warning that multiplayer factories introduce unresolved technical and organizational dynamics.

videos.title: Your Sub-Agents Are a Distributed System. Treat Them Like One. - Girish Konda, Microsoft
videos.overview: Girish Konda argues that orchestrators, concurrent sub-agents, shared context, and tool side effects form a distributed system, even when the interface looks like a simple text-returning function. He proposes SAFE handoffs: source-aware facts, at-most-once effects, bounded fan-out, and explicit outcomes enforced by orchestration code.
key_points: A fluent sub-agent response can conceal partial execution, unsupported inference, or no execution at all. A timeout likewise cannot establish whether work failed, remains in progress, or completed without a delivered reply.
Shared context can turn an unchecked claim into apparently corroborated evidence. Several agents repeating one shared source do not constitute independent verification or a meaningful quorum.
Facts should carry provenance, source version, scope, and relevant times. Freshness must be checked when a fact is used, not assumed because it was recently copied.
Every side effect needs an identity and an approval bound to the exact action. An uncertain write should be read back by identity rather than blindly replayed.
Downstream concurrency needs capacity gates, bounded waits, and explicit refusals. Capacity must be reserved before starting work to avoid check-then-act races.
Structured outcomes such as partial, stale, and unknown must be validated in code alongside evidence and numerical claims; a warning paragraph is not an enforcement boundary.
SAFE is a single-orchestrator design, not a universal consistency protocol. It does not guarantee truthful sources, exactly-once delivery, automatic rollback, or a global order across workers.
summary: Konda starts from an ordinary multi-agent setup: an orchestrator delegates concurrent work, workers read shared repositories or context, and their tools touch databases, APIs, CI, or deployment systems. That is already a distributed system, but a string-in/string-out interface hides familiar failure modes. A worker may stop halfway and still return polished success text, while a timeout cannot distinguish slow work, a crash, or a lost reply. His alert-analysis illustration makes the epistemic problem concrete: genuine telemetry analysis, recognition of a familiar title, and outright hallucination can all produce the same confident conclusion. He recommends making failure a structured value containing status, completed and incomplete work, evidence, and side effects, while preserving the difference between checking a condition and finding it false versus being unable to check.

Shared mutable context creates a second problem: an inferred claim can be copied into a review and a runbook, leaving three agreeing artifacts that all descend from one unsupported sentence. Asking more agents does not fix this dependence. Konda therefore proposes SAFE handoffs, beginning with source reads. Claims become records carrying source identity and version, scope, and times describing when data was current, read, and used. Freshness is checked at the decision point; an earlier observation can become unusable even when its wording remains unchanged. The aim is to preserve provenance and causal relationships rather than impose a universal ordering on every worker. Keeping workers attached to one orchestrator provides a practical coordination point for the session and causal guarantees he wants.

The next two elements concern side effects and capacity. At-most-once effects require identifying each action, binding approval to that exact action, and reading back the resulting state. If a tool creates a pull request but its reply disappears, repeating the entire delegated task may create a duplicate. His MCP pacemaker bridge therefore distinguishes safely replaying initialization from replaying an uncertain tool call, which it avoids. He applies fencing-token reasoning to resumed agents: old authority must not silently authorize a new write. Fan-out budgets address failures caused by concurrency itself. In his bridge, simultaneous package-manager cold starts contended over a shared cache. He introduced a default gate allowing two such starts, a bounded wait with a documented availability-oriented escape, and a separate session cap. Capacity must be reserved before starting work, not checked afterward.

Explicit outcomes complete the model. The orchestrator validates schemas, evidence, freshness, and calculations in code, refusing unsupported results instead of forwarding them with cautionary prose. One example rejects an improvement claim because lower raw error counts do not imply a lower error rate when request volume also changes. Konda emphasizes the limits: provenance makes a claim inspectable, not necessarily true; a lost reply remains unknown until verified; compensating actions must be designed separately; and SAFE supplies no global order across workers. Stronger checks also cost reads, latency, and operational ownership of refusals. He deliberately favors consistency for writes while accepting an availability tradeoff for cold starts. The pattern is aimed at agents affecting real systems under one orchestrator; human-reviewed drafting may not justify the overhead, and decentralized multi-orchestrator systems need a different design.

videos.title: Your PR Says the Tests Passed. Prove It. - Stephen Chin & Cassandra Chin
videos.overview: Stephen and Cassandra Chin present an evidence-first approach to writing pull requests with Trace Tune and the embedded graph database Relate. Their central claim is that deterministic preparation of connected execution evidence can improve PR accuracy while reducing repeated model-based research and token use.
key_points: A correct code change can still receive a poor review when its PR description misstates tests, omits command context, or makes unsupported claims.
Session memory and code diffs are insufficient provenance: compressed context can lose execution details, while a diff does not explain which checks actually ran against the submitted content.
The original iterative research-and-review workflow still made mistakes, including a test-evidence example involving commands that needed to run sequentially.
Relate constructs an evidence graph and retrieves a connected neighborhood brief linking rationale, code, checks, and source attribution before drafting begins.
The presenters retain a stronger writing model but use cheaper reviewers for focused evidence checking, arguing that prose quality and mechanical verification need different capabilities.
They report modest PRBench score improvements and approximately half the previous token use, while providing no detailed statistical basis for generalizing those results.
Optional comics communicate the change playfully, but the technical contribution is a compact, attributable evidence packet shared by the writer and reviewers.
summary: The Chins frame pull-request quality as an evidence problem rather than simply a code-generation problem. A change may be useful while its description contains incorrect test claims, missing preview links, or unclear command attribution. An agent asked to summarize its own session often relies on a large context window that has already been compressed, making important details less dependable. A diff-based description has another limitation: it explains changed lines without establishing how the work was performed or verified. Cassandra connects this concern to earlier education work, where a submitted program did not reveal the prompting and effort behind it. Trace Tune applies that tracing idea to reconstruct what happened across relevant agent sessions.

The initial workflow finds branch-related traces, researches them, drafts a description, reviews it, and loops with additional context. The presenters say this already improved PRs, but further iterations could still introduce or preserve errors. Their concrete example involves a test command and a TypeScript-checking command that, in that case, needed to run sequentially rather than concurrently. The narration is inconsistent about the draft's exact original wording, but the failure concerns inaccurate interpretation of execution evidence. Merely finding command names in a trace is not enough to justify a successful-check claim. Repeatedly asking agents to reconstruct the history also increases token costs. Substituting a cheaper writer did not solve their combined accuracy and communication problem.

Their revised approach moves evidence assembly into Relate, described as an open-source, Rust-based embedded graph database. Relationships connect the reason for a change, affected code, checks, and the underlying sources. A neighborhood query produces a compact, connected brief before the writer starts, reducing the need for fresh model-driven investigation on every revision. The same packet supports focused reviewer checks, including missing findings and unsupported assertions. They retain a stronger writer while using cheaper reviewers because, in their experiments, weaker writers tended to turn feedback into mechanical checklists rather than clear explanations. One illustrated output ties a working-directory change to its exception rules and distinguishes checks performed on submitted content from earlier activity.

The presenters evaluate the approach with PRBench, combining audit traces, code, model judges, and human checking. They report score changes around 74 to 76 and 82 to 86 on a hundred-point scale, alongside approximately halved token use compared with the earlier workflow. These are project-specific reported results, not evidence that graphs universally improve agent systems. The mechanism they emphasize is reusable, however: perform relationship lookup and evidence curation with local computation, then ask models to write and verify against the resulting packet. This reduces duplicated research rather than merely buying cheaper inference. They close by recommending Trace Tune and Relate for similar evidence-heavy work; optional comics are an additional presentation feature, not a substitute for accurate claims and attributable verification.

videos.title: Your Agent Hates Your CLI - Ayush Bhardwaj, Allos AI
videos.overview: Ayush Bhardwaj shows how the shell commands agents write around a CLI reveal missing product features and sometimes conceal failures. Using his cross-tool session-history CLI as a case study, he turns repeated filtering, JSON processing, and manual batching into interface changes and transcript-derived regression tests.
key_points: Across roughly 20,000 calls involving 14 CLIs in his transcripts, about a quarter piped output into filters; some read-heavy commands exceeded half.
Repeated pipelines are behavioral feedback: selecting surrounding messages suggests slice controls, Python over JSON suggests compact fields, and shell loops suggest batching.
Pipelines can hide both failure status and error text. Without pipefail, a successful final filter can make a failed upstream command appear successful.
Skills, help text, and error messages are part of the agent interface. A stale instruction caused a removed flag to persist in all 95 observed searches.
After new selection features and updated instructions reached agents, his tool's piping rate fell from roughly 82% to about a quarter.
Replay real commands as evaluations, hold some cases back, and measure correct answers and interaction turns rather than assuming fewer output tokens mean lower cost or latency.
summary: Bhardwaj argues that agents rarely report usability problems directly: they compensate by writing programs around your program. His examples include trimming documentation, taking the end of a vulnerability report, and extracting the tail of test output. Each workaround assumes where the answer appears. In approximately 20,000 calls across 14 CLIs from his own transcripts, about a quarter used output filters. More importantly, 83% of pipelines belonged to patterns observed at least ten times, suggesting recurring interface needs rather than isolated improvisation.

His session-history CLI provided a concrete redesign exercise. Agents frequently filtered full-session reads to find the relevant messages, processed JSON to reduce fields, and looped over sessions to inspect several individually. He translated those behaviors into match-centered reading, matching-message and trailing-message selection, compact search output, and batched inspection. Output caps alone were insufficient: limiting size does not identify relevance. The safety problem is equally important. A pipeline can return the final filter's successful status despite an upstream failure, and truncation can remove the error that would otherwise alert the model.

Features only help when agents know to use them. Bhardwaj deliberately left a no-longer-functional flag in his skill instructions and observed it in all 95 subsequent searches. After rewritten instructions loaded in two sessions, the flag disappeared and agents immediately tried the new controls. He reports that piping fell substantially after the redesign and instruction updates. This makes documentation maintenance a behavioral correctness issue: agents can faithfully execute obsolete guidance instead of discovering a better interface themselves.

For evaluation, he recommends replaying commands against old and new builds and using the agent's next action as an imperfect indication of what it wanted. Ranking changes should preserve useful results; formatting changes should retain needed information; some cases should remain held out. He also cautions against optimizing token counts in isolation: a database CLI example cut tool-output volume substantially without improving overall cost or runtime because that output was a small share of total context. Humans should define the intended interface, then use agents and real transcripts to test it.

videos.title: Your Agent Doesn't Need an LLM for Every Decision - Raymond Weitekamp, OpenProse
videos.overview: Raymond Weitekamp proposes recursive decision models: systems that navigate tasks through small, fast judgments, calling generative models only when generation is needed. Through game, smart-home, and real-time audio examples, he develops a decision-first architecture and connects it to an unfinished voice-driven computer-use project called OSO.
key_points: Decision models rank or select supplied options rather than generate arbitrary text. The surrounding code still determines how those judgments become actions.

Recursive decision models keep context outside the model, allow decisions to invoke further decisions within a depth limit, and must work without generation while remaining composable with LLMs and agents.
Hierarchical product search, image subdivision, Doom, and Factorio illustrate how many small classifications can produce behavior that might otherwise be assigned to a reasoning model.
Decision-only systems depend on having available actions enumerated by code, an application, or another agent. They cannot invent an absent action or procedure by selection alone.
A shared map connects decision and generative components: decision models select named operations, while an LLM can add or modify the structured operations and their compositions.
An arbiter controls which parallel or speculative decisions may mutate state, preventing competing decision streams from independently executing conflicting actions.

The earshot audio demonstration explores teaching a tiny real-time model and deciding when to trust it. OSO extends this direction toward voice-first computer control that delegates to larger agents when necessary.
summary: Weitekamp begins with the distinction between fast judgments and open-ended generation, borrowing the system-one/system-two framing associated with Thinking, Fast and Slow. His central question is whether tasks that appear to require deliberate reasoning can sometimes be solved through many small, rapid decisions. Generative models expand possibilities; decision models converge by ranking or choosing supplied alternatives. These are complementary operations, not interchangeable products. His recursive decision model, or RDM, adapts the structure of recursive language models: context remains external, code supplies relevant slices, and a decision can invoke another decision until a configured depth limit. He deliberately requires the architecture to function without any generative model before adding generation back as an optional capability.

The examples explore different ways to compose that structure. A modified Galton-board visualization replaces random bounces with classifications, illustrating hierarchical sorting rather than a necessary optimization. Product-category search narrows a hierarchy of roughly 12,000 categories instead of exposing every category at once; code chooses whether to follow one branch or several. Image examples similarly subdivide or zoom into candidate regions, although he acknowledges that a capable vision model might answer some examples directly. Doom combines moment-to-moment action selection with a separate exploration policy. His Factorio demonstration locates a faulty production component through successive decisions and dispatches an action to repair it, without generative language calls. Its inefficient route also exposes a missing planning component. These demonstrations support an architectural possibility, not a claim that recursion universally beats simpler classifiers.

The boundary is the action vocabulary: a selector cannot choose an operation nobody supplied. Games and browsers may nevertheless expose enough programmatically enumerable actions for decision-first control to be useful. For less predefined behavior, Weitekamp introduces a shared map of named operations, descriptions, and executable functions. A decision model can select an existing operation; an LLM can structurally edit the map or create compositions, such as making movie time mean switching on the television and dimming lights. Another component, the arbiter, handles concurrency. Cheap decision calls can run speculatively in parallel, but their outputs must not all change state independently. The arbiter gates execution based on available information and confidence, separating parallel judgments from permission to act. He describes an initial structured Python-framework implementation and a standalone Rust package as ways to experiment with these ideas.

The final section connects this architecture to physical interaction with computers. Drawing on laptop-orchestra work and earlier real-time musical interfaces, Weitekamp wants to reduce dependence on keyboards and mice that cause him discomfort. In the earshot demonstration, a slower transcription-based path supplies supervision to a tiny audio classifier working on short sound windows. A separate trust decision determines when the system can follow that smaller model; he reports the demonstration reaching approximately 45-millisecond response times. He also highlights Hunch's local doodle classification as another example of small models enabling responsive interfaces. His unfinished OSO project applies the same principle to voice-driven computer use: begin with decisions, learn preferences, shift familiar tasks toward the smallest trusted model, and delegate generative work to conventional coding agents when needed. The ambition is an adaptive interface, not evidence that general hands-free computer control is already solved.

videos.title: You Can't Tell What an Agent Skill Will Do by Reading It - Roey Ben Chaim, Zenity
videos.overview: Roey Ben Chaim explains why inspecting a skill's initial instructions cannot establish what it will actually execute. Zenity's detonation chamber combines realistic environments, varied task trajectories and machine-level telemetry to investigate dependencies, credential theft and behavior that survives beyond the visible skill.
key_points: Sensitive access is not sufficient evidence of maliciousness: an official Azure diagnostic skill may legitimately inspect cloud configuration and identity information. Investigators must relate actions to the user's task and authorization.

Static review misses externally loaded instructions, changing remote content and dependency behavior. A model reviewing the skill can also accept misleading explanations contained in the material under review.
Useful dynamic testing requires both an appropriate environment and relevant tasks. The chamber uses a world builder to supply dependencies and an operator to exercise different skill trajectories.

Conversation traces omit effects produced by installations and subprocesses. Process creation, filesystem activity and network capture help connect an agent's apparent actions to actual machine behavior.
Reported findings include substituted dependencies, persistence after removal, replacement of an official skill creator and a Paperclip impersonation campaign connected to credential harvesting.

The reported 1.7 million downloads measure distribution, not confirmed compromise. Ben Chaim's practical conclusion is to treat skills as package dependencies with restricted access, recursively inspected inputs and runtime observation.
summary: Ben Chaim frames skills as third-party capabilities that introduce instructions, resources and sometimes executable code. Their actions cannot be judged without understanding the task: an official Azure diagnostic may legitimately access information that malware also targets. Static inspection has another boundary problem. The installed document can load dependencies or remote instructions that the reviewer never sees, and external content can change later. Automated model review is not decisive either, because explanations supplied by an attacker are not independent evidence of authorization.

Zenity therefore built a detonation chamber that runs an agent with a skill inside a sandbox. The initial version lacked realistic dependencies and sufficiently varied prompts. A world builder now prepares the services, CLIs and project context a skill needs; an operator selects tasks intended to exercise different routes. Safeguard refusals remain an evidentiary limit: a stopped test is not proof that the skill completed safely. The chamber also records process creation, filesystem activity and network traffic, capturing installation side effects that conversation traces can miss.

Ben Chaim reports finding 100 malicious skills among thousands and having them removed from skills.sh. Examples include an unofficial Polymarket-related dependency that collected sensitive information, skills that returned after removal and a third-party skill creator replacing the official version. A Paperclip impersonation campaign allegedly disguised attacker-controlled communication as application logging and harvested local authentication material. Related skills reportedly accumulated around 1.7 million downloads, although that does not establish how many systems executed the behavior or lost credentials. He says reporting the campaign to Vercel and Microsoft led to takedowns within twelve hours.

The broader lesson is that the agent supply chain includes everything entering its context, not merely installed skills: websites, database rows, packages and comments can all influence behavior. Review should follow what a skill actually loads, distinguish legitimate sensitive work from unauthorized access and preserve evidence connecting effects to their causes. Runtime testing complements inspection rather than proving universal safety; outcomes depend on the environment, exercised task and agent decisions. Least privilege and observation remain necessary even when the initial skill looks familiar.

videos.title: The Agents Were Fine. Everything Around Them Broke. - Joey Wang, Harvey
videos.overview: Joey Wang recounts how Harvey's internal Spectre platform encountered bottlenecks around coding agents rather than inside the models. Follow-up loops, callable infrastructure, duplicate suppression and fair scheduling helped the platform absorb more work, but rising PR volume exposed an unresolved merge bottleneck.
key_points: Spectre runs developers' preferred agents while providing shared cloud environments, secrets, project knowledge, checks and audit trails. Wang describes roughly 10,000 agent-written PRs and around 460 users in the reported month.
A follow-up loop responds to CI failures and continues fixing changes after initial code generation. Four out of five merged backend agent PRs in the cited month had passed through that loop.
Making UI actions callable through a CLI enabled laptop agents, sandbox agents and CI to initiate work. Command-line usage grew from one task in May to around 6,500 tasks in October.
An alert workflow launched roughly 900 tasks for one underlying bug. Associating repeat alerts with an existing investigation prevented duplicate agent work.
A separate burst of about 950 CLI tasks exhausted shared capacity. A fair launch queue added capacity-aware dispatch, interactive priority, fair shares and visible queue positions.
Automation needs guardrails before widespread adoption: repeated failures disable an automation, and budgets or expiry dates can bound unattended work.

Merge remains unresolved. Wang reports a roughly 60% monthly rise in company PRs and longer merge times, while only about one in twenty merges carried the demonstrated proof-of-functionality he wants to make standard.
summary: Wang describes Spectre as infrastructure beneath developers' preferred coding agents, not a replacement for them. Harvey supplies the cloud environment, secrets, real stack, project knowledge, checks and audit trail. He reports about 10,000 agent-written PRs and roughly 460 users in the cited month, with work expanding into data questions and marketing requests. Shared projects give specialized testing knowledge a persistent home, let teams pin trusted skills and keep different agents operating under common rules.

The highest-value workflow continues after code generation. An agent can investigate an alert, test against a real stack and attach evidence to a PR; a follow-up loop reads CI failures and attempts repairs. Human review remains, with notifications aligned to working hours and merging after approval. Wang says four out of five merged backend agent PRs in the cited month used this loop. Exposing UI capabilities through a CLI also let other agents initiate work, reaching around 6,500 monthly terminal-started tasks. Caching repository copies addressed checkout overhead that had exceeded a minute on average.

Greater accessibility created capacity failures. A bug emitted alerts across workspaces, and an automation launched roughly 900 tasks in four hours to investigate the same problem. Repeat alerts now join an existing investigation. Later, an engineer submitted about 950 CLI tasks in three hours, filling the cluster and blocking colleagues. The response was a fair launch queue: requests receive queue positions, dispatch waits for capacity, interactive work gets priority and users receive fair shares while borrowing spare capacity. These incidents required duplicate suppression and admission control, not better code generation.

The bottleneck then moved downstream. Company PR volume reportedly rose around 60% in a month, merge times grew from fifteen to thirty minutes to over an hour, and the merge queue became unreliable. Wang explicitly says this remains unsolved. Meanwhile, unattended automations gained adoption, prompting automatic shutdown after five consecutive failures and optional budgets or expiry dates. His next questions concern persistent channel agents and stronger proof before human review; only about one in twenty merges currently carries that evidence. The closing lesson is to own post-generation completion, expose actions programmatically and constrain every source of task creation before it overwhelms shared infrastructure.

videos.title: Merge Is the Bottleneck - Prasanna Sankar, Vorflux
videos.overview: Prasanna Sankar describes a sequence of bottlenecks that appears as coding agents become capable of longer, parallel work: environment setup, planning, testing, review, merge and eventually project management. His proposed next step is a goal-directed coworker that detects actionable intent in company events and starts bounded work instead of waiting for manually assigned tasks.
key_points: Moving agents to the cloud requires reproducing the working environment, including dependent services, ports, authentication and seed data; running only the edited service leaves testing incomplete.
The platform spends additional inference compute on parallel exploration and detailed planning, then uses dependency graphs to distribute independent implementation work.
End-to-end completion includes browser testing, inspectable evidence, configurable model reviews and a merge queue that keeps changes aligned with the main branch.

Sankar says greater parallelism shifts the human bottleneck from code production to tracking, initiating and landing useful work. Customer calls and alerts already contain much of the intent needed to begin incremental tasks.
Unbounded event-driven automation can flood reviewers, generate noisy notifications, suppress symptoms instead of fixing causes and consume tokens on unwanted work.
His Autobots model assigns a goal and communication channel, connects relevant events and increases autonomy within observable budgets and approval boundaries.
He distinguishes human-led zero-to-one judgment from incremental work with existing intent. The zero-employee company is presented as a directional ambition, not an achieved operating model.
summary: Sankar presents the product as an attempt to maximize personal leverage rather than merely accelerate typing. He argues that longer-running agents belong in the cloud, but only after reproducing the environment that makes local development useful. His team invests up front in configuring machines, dependent services, ports, authentication and seed data. Without that setup, a cloud agent may edit code while remaining unable to validate it against the real application. The opening competitive-programming background motivates his preference for spending more inference compute to reduce human effort; it is not a benchmark comparison of the resulting product.

The first platform version addresses the development workflow as a chain of bottlenecks. Parallel exploration agents produce detailed architecture and a summarized plan, reducing repeated human planning exchanges. A dependency graph then assigns independent implementation work to subagents. Browser and end-to-end tests run remotely, with videos or staging links letting users inspect whether a feature works without returning to localhost. Configurable reviewers can examine different concerns or use a different model from the builder. Finally, a merge queue rebases changes and lands them. In this account, implementation speed matters only if the surrounding system can turn generated work into tested, reviewed changes.

Once these pieces worked, Sankar says concurrency increased from a few desktop tasks to twenty or thirty cloud tasks, exposing a project-management limit. Humans still had to remember tasks, initiate sessions, track ownership and ensure useful completion. He proposes extracting incremental intent directly from customer conversations, alerts and other company signals, while reserving genuinely novel zero-to-one decisions for human taste and judgment. Simply connecting every event to an agent is insufficient: he describes floods of unmerged PRs, constant interruptions, superficial alert silencing and runaway spending. His alternative resembles supervising a new employee: start with bounded responsibility, require early check-ins, observe results and adjust autonomy within a budget.

The second version implements this idea through Autobots with goals, home channels and event connections. Examples include on-call triage, CI improvement and a project manager reporting blockers and requesting reviews. In a customer-call anecdote, a bot identifies a bug from the transcript and screen share, asks permission, involves the responsible engineer, follows the PR through deployment and drafts a customer update for approval. Sankar also proposes routing well-specified work to cheaper open models while reserving frontier models for judgment and communication. His endpoint is a company organized around self-starting operational loops, with people creating new capabilities and deciding what matters. He explicitly acknowledges mistakes and responsibilities that are not ready to delegate; the zero-employee company remains a north star.

videos.title: Give Your On-Call Its Own AI Teammate - Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi & Vlad Tsvang, Meta
videos.overview: Meta's incident-tooling engineers describe a persistent AI teammate owned by an on-call rotation rather than an individual engineer. The design combines cross-signal investigation, shared memory, explicit approval gates, and selective autonomy to reduce the number of items humans must drive to completion.
key_points: A reactive assistant can answer incident questions while leaving the human responsible for choosing every next step; the proposed teammate begins work when signals arrive.
One rotation-level agent connects alerts, tickets, deployments, incident history, and team knowledge instead of leaving separate bots with isolated context.
The autonomy ladder moves from read-only investigation to approved changes to independently handling selected low-criticality work; high-criticality decisions remain human-owned.
Advancement depends on mistake cost, detectability through tests or review, and demonstrated performance on the specific action, not blanket trust in the agent.
Scheduled health checks recover stuck automation, while shift handoffs and morning digests surface actionable decisions rather than requiring constant board monitoring.
Team-scoped identity, configurable skills, inspectable trajectories, and memory updated by corrections support continuity across engineers and rotations.
The speakers report promising early signs but withhold numerical time-savings claims pending rigorous measurement; code fixes still require normal human review and CI.
summary: The speakers distinguish useful incident assistance from ownership of the operational workflow. In their simplified checkout example, a conventional assistant finds metrics, a deployment, and a runbook only after the engineer asks each question. A persistent teammate instead groups related alerts, connects a configuration change with past incidents, and prepares a hypothesis, verification step, and proposed fix before the human engages. The intended shift is from manually coordinating disconnected tools to reviewing a prepared decision with linked evidence.

They organize permissions as an autonomy ladder modeled on onboarding an engineer. Level one investigates without changing anything. Level two drafts fixes, test plans, and responses to review comments, but requires human approval before production changes. Level three handles selected low-criticality work and escalates consequential decisions. Promotion depends on how costly an error would be, how readily existing checks would detect it, and the agent's record on that particular action. Autonomy therefore varies by task; it is not a universal setting. The speakers emphasize that most drafted fixes do not land and that review remains the filter.

The surrounding system makes continuous operation practical. Incoming signals are classified and routed to incident investigation, team agents, coding sessions, memory, or code search. A separate scheduled process checks for failed or stuck runs and attempts recovery, escalating when it cannot repair them. A shared board tracks progress, while chat and incident interfaces expose evidence and approval actions. Morning digests and shift handoffs summarize completed work, ongoing investigations, and the smaller queue requiring human input rather than making engineers monitor every execution.

Continuity comes from one identity, configuration, and memory per rotation. An engineer's correction can inform the next person's shift, and feedback reopens the relevant item rather than being treated as a detached comment. The speakers describe semantic retrieval, scoring whether memories helped, and promoting or retiring entries. Teams supply their own playbooks and trusted skills without forking the underlying agent. Their next priorities are measuring actual on-call time saved, learning from whether mitigations receive approval, enabling chat-authored skills, and earning medium-criticality autonomy through evidence rather than granting it prematurely.

videos.title: Every Correction You Give Your Agent Is Data - Brian Douglas, Paper Compute
videos.overview: Brian Douglas treats engineers' corrections to coding agents as a dataset of organizational knowledge that ordinary compilation and automated review miss. His Rust-review prototype illustrates how captured sessions can become reusable skills, evaluations, and eventually a specialized reviewer, with skills recommended as the starting point.
key_points: An agent can generate compiling code while violating decisions about API structure, service boundaries, or existing libraries; an experienced engineer's pushback exposes those missing constraints.
Douglas's own limited professional Rust experience makes this knowledge gap concrete: he often accepts generated code that his teammates subsequently challenge during review.
Capture and label agent sessions, including pushback, apologies, exemplary sessions, and regressions, rather than relying exclusively on GitHub review comments.
His Twin Review prototype uses labeled traces and post-training to approximate a teammate's review preferences; he clarifies that it is not open source because it contains sensitive data.
Start by extracting skills from traces, then build evaluations before considering specialized fine-tuning or preference optimization.
Local trace storage can support the workflow without the Paper console; Douglas describes Tapes using a local Postgres database.
summary: Douglas frames agent-assisted development as both a productivity opportunity and a learning problem. Drawing on Rick Rubin's creative-production analogy and Addy Osmani's writing about junior engineers losing practice, he asks what happens when agents perform the repetitions that previously built engineering judgment. His own situation makes the question concrete: he uses Rust at Paper Compute but lacks the professional experience to reliably challenge generated Rust. Code that compiles and receives a favorable automated review can still attract substantial objections from experienced teammates.

Those objections are the useful data. A teammate's correction may explain an intentional API boundary, identify a duplicated service, or point out an existing Go testing library that the agent has started rebuilding. Douglas captures sessions through Tapes and demonstrates centralized inspection and labels in the Paper console. He argues that collecting harness conversations matters because review increasingly happens inside coding tools rather than as durable GitHub comments. Without session capture, the reasoning behind corrections can disappear even when the final code survives.

His demonstration turns labeled traces into Twin Review, a command-line reviewer that comments on a pull request as though it were his teammate Matt. Douglas describes post-training on Matt's pushback in Go and Rust sessions, not on GitHub review history.
