At team scale, manager sessions and builders communicate across sessions to unblock dependencies. A dedicated merge coordinator handles the flood of pull requests and shared integration concerns, including conflicting database migration numbers, alongside GitHub merge queues. Carson presents cloud execution as essential to his approach, but that is his operational preference rather than a demonstrated comparison with local alternatives. He also acknowledges a balance between extensive review and keeping the merge queue moving.

His hiring process evaluates observable agent operation before conversational impressions. Candidates first submit an unpaid, roughly forty-five-minute whole-screen recording of shipping a feature pull request, usually in an application they already maintain. A ranking agent reviews recordings and transcripts; the top five are invited to a paid sixteen-hour project using the company's coding platform, under an NDA, to prepare real work for merging. Loom recordings provide further evidence, and finalist conversations happen afterward. Carson reports that this process works better for him, but supports that conclusion with personal experience rather than controlled hiring outcomes.

videos.title: Engineering Agency out of the Happy Path — Matthew Jewkes, Standard Cybernetics
videos.overview: Matthew Jewkes argues that enterprise AI should remove routine demands on expert judgment rather than create another stream of agent notifications. His biopharmaceutical indexing case study shows how routing ambiguous, novel, and business-critical cases separately can support reliable automation while turning exceptions into useful business intelligence.
key_points: Cheaper execution can increase the demand for judgment: producing more work is not the same as freeing experts to decide what matters.
Full automation removes humans from routine processing while retaining explicit escape routes for unusual, adversarial, uncertain, or business-critical inputs.
Distinguish actual mistakes from unresolved organizational definitions and genuinely novel cases. Better model performance alone cannot resolve all three categories.
The reported high accuracy came from narrowing and routing the task distribution, then investing heavily in evaluations and performance improvement on the business-critical subset.
Organized exception queues can expose emerging customer needs, while organized ambiguity can help leaders identify low-value work worth suspending rather than specifying.
Choose established, detail-oriented processes with material revenue and visible customer pain. Discovery work and subjective judgment generally benefit more from human flexibility.
summary: Jewkes starts with an organizational bottleneck: domain experts spend their weeks reconstructing context, handling interruptions, and deciding matters that could have been routine. As execution becomes cheaper, he expects judgment to become more constrained. His proposed response is full automation, with no human involvement on the happy path. AI still exercises agency at the boundaries, checking whether inputs belong in the process and escalating uncertainty instead of pushing unexpected situations through a brittle workflow.

His case study concerns indexing documents and relationships in a large biopharmaceutical information business. An initial agent-like implementation reached roughly 80–83% performance, but expert review revealed several different problems hidden inside that score. Some answers were simply wrong; others depended on definitions the organization had not settled; genuinely new science required changes to the indexing ontology. One example asks whether a downstream biological effect counts as a drug target. Another involves Verve 102 and mechanisms requiring new classification decisions. These cases needed different handling, not one undifferentiated improvement loop.

The team therefore invested heavily in routing, separating ambiguity and novelty from ordinary processing and sending business-critical tasks through a more thoroughly tested pipeline. Jewkes reports improving the selected critical workload from about 95% to around 99.95%, deploying only after a random-sample comparison favored it over historical human work. His claim of outperforming PhD experts is explicitly about repetitive work at scale, including fatigue and time pressure, not an expert studying one case carefully. Bringing experts prepared examples also proved more productive than asking them to populate blank evaluation spreadsheets.

Routing created a second benefit: experts could review grouped exceptions rather than encounter them sporadically. Ambiguous, marginally valuable work could be frozen until a business case emerged; clusters of novel cases could reveal investment opportunities and prepare experts for customer conversations. Jewkes describes an eight-figure account where this structured attention helped. He nevertheless treats full automation as a substantial capital and organizational investment, requiring extensive evaluation, trust building, ownership changes, and commercial coordination. His closing prediction is that managing collective attention will matter more than choosing a differentiated orchestration framework.

videos.title: Can AI Agents Beat Wall Street at Predicting Earnings? - Ashwin Paranjape, Samaya AI
videos.overview: Ashwin Paranjape presents earnings forecasting as a more interpretable test of financial agents than stock-price prediction. Samaya's reported experiments suggest that frontier models can improve on analyst consensus when equipped with current, point-in-time data, but the examples also show that finding evidence and acting on it are different capabilities.
key_points: Quarterly earnings provide numerical outcomes, an expert baseline in analyst consensus, and subsequent management explanations. This makes it easier to investigate whether an agent reached the right answer for defensible reasons than with noisy stock-price movements.

The evaluation harness adapts Samaya's production research tools and enforces a historical information cutoff through authenticated, programmatic access controls. Timestamped news streams substitute for unrestricted web access, where historical information boundaries are harder to enforce.

Across more than 450 earnings events and seven models, the speaker reports stronger results from newer models on normalized prediction error, beat-or-miss direction, and surprise correlation. Revenue provides the clearest reported improvement over bias-corrected consensus.

The talk distinguishes ordinary consensus from a baseline adjusted for companies' tendency to beat estimates. Reported normalized errors are 1.5 for ordinary consensus and 1.18 after bias correction, making the corrected baseline a more demanding comparison.

Successful research can uncover indirect evidence, such as a supplier's disclosures, and propagate its implications into a financial forecast. A contrasting Ross Stores example shows an agent identifying a peer's tariff refund but declining to incorporate that evidence into its margin prediction.

Ablations indicate that current data matters substantially: model-only knowledge performs poorly, and data from eleven weeks before earnings produces materially worse results. Expert guidance increases research effort, while the strongest tested models show little degradation when consensus references are removed.
summary: Paranjape argues that earnings forecasting is a better starting point for evaluating financial reasoning than predicting stock prices. Price movements are noisy and often difficult to explain, whereas quarterly reports supply actual revenue, margins, income, and earnings per share. Analyst consensus provides a human comparison, and management commentary offers evidence about why surprises occurred. The research question therefore becomes whether agents can anticipate financial outcomes and produce reasoning that survives comparison with subsequent disclosures.

Samaya builds the experiment around a historical research environment rather than a model answering from memory. Company documents, prices, consensus, and news are restricted to information available before the prediction deadline. An authenticated gate enforces this boundary across retrieval and structured-data tools; timestamped news substitutes for unrestricted web search. The speaker reports evaluating seven models across more than 450 earnings events after the latest tested model's stated training cutoff. Measures include volatility-normalized error, surprise direction, and correlation between predicted and actual surprise magnitude.

Newer models reportedly improve against consensus, with revenue showing particularly strong results against a bias-corrected baseline. The examples explain what improvement can involve. In one semiconductor case, an agent finds evidence in a small UK wafer supplier's disclosures, connects it to stronger data-center business, and carries the adjustment through the profit-and-loss forecast. In the Ross Stores counterexample, the agent notices a peer's tariff refund but excludes its implications from the margin estimate. Evidence retrieval succeeds, but forecast adjustment fails.

The ablations shift attention from model rankings to the surrounding system. Parametric knowledge alone is inadequate, and stale information substantially reduces performance. Expert guidance encourages longer research and improves one leading model's error. Removing consensus references has little reported effect on the strongest model, suggesting that it can reconstruct a baseline view within this setup. The closing agenda includes customer-specific data, studying whether agents reason differently from humans, and learning from past errors. These are forecasting results, not a demonstrated stock-trading strategy.

videos.title: AI Writes Code Faster Than Uber Can Merge It - Preetam Dwivedi & Manjari Akella, Uber
videos.overview: Preetam Dwivedi and Manjari Akella explain how AI-driven change volume overwhelmed Uber's existing merge-queue design. Their response combines traffic shaping, automatic deferral, and selective relaxation of integration checks, trading an always-green raw trunk for higher throughput backed by post-merge validation and a separately tracked verified state.
key_points: Uber reports more than 5,000 developers working across six language-based monorepositories, producing over 36,000 commits and 27,000 pull requests weekly. The talk concentrates on Go, where the speakers encountered their largest scaling challenges.

Independent green pull-request builds do not establish that changes will work together. Uber's merge queue tests prospective integration states, using target analysis, probabilistic speculation, and bypassing slow large changes to increase throughput while protecting trunk.

The speakers attribute growing queue pressure primarily to AI-generated changes: requests rose from roughly 90 per hour in January 2026 to 130 in March, while P95 landing time deteriorated from 30 minutes to three or four hours.

Admission gating protects peak-hour capacity by separating small changes from expensive, broadly affecting changes. It raises reported throughput to about 160 lands per hour but disadvantages developers whose normal work touches shared libraries or large portions of the build graph.

A persistent deferred queue replaces rejection with automatic later admission when capacity permits. This removes the need for developers to retry at inconvenient times, but does not itself eliminate their waiting time.

Conflict relaxation ranks overlaps using target and dependency information, preserves stronger relationships, and drops weaker edges to restore parallelism. Assigning relationships when requests arrive avoids repeatedly invalidating previously scheduled speculative work.

Relaxation permits some untested combinations to reach main, so a post-merge validator maintains a separate verified-main pointer and pages on-call when validation fails. The final reported peak is roughly 300 lands per hour with P95 landing time back at 30 minutes; recovery still requires manual fixes or reverts.
summary: The speakers begin with a distributed-development problem: two pull requests can each pass against the same base and still break the repository when combined. Uber's merge queue addresses this by validating prospective integration states rather than assuming independent CI success is sufficient. Its existing optimizations include separating changes with nonoverlapping build targets, prioritizing speculative builds using historical success and change characteristics, and allowing smaller changes to bypass slow large ones. These techniques supported a green trunk under earlier demand. As AI-generated changes increased, however, requests rose from roughly 90 per hour in January 2026 to 130 in March. Keeping the same validation guarantees pushed P95 landing time from 30 minutes to three or four hours.

The first response controls admission. Small changes affecting fewer targets continue into the active queue during peak hours, while expensive changes are held back because their broad dependencies consume capacity and constrain other work. The speakers report an increase to about 160 lands per hour, but acknowledge an uneven burden: shared-library developers are especially likely to produce expensive changes. Initially, those developers must return outside peak hours and retry. A persistent deferred queue improves that experience by accepting the request once and automatically releasing it when admission rules permit. This is a scheduling improvement rather than a latency cure; the change still waits, but the developer no longer has to arrange their day around manually finding capacity.

The larger throughput improvement comes from weakening the queue's conflict graph. Under strict target analysis, a chain of overlapping changes can form one connected component and constrain parallel execution. Conflict relaxation replaces a binary overlap decision with a continuous strength score, using Jaccard-style target overlap and information about newly introduced dependency edges. Strong links remain; selected weak links are removed to achieve a configured degree of parallelism. Uber makes these assignments when a new request enters instead of continually recomputing the entire graph, preserving useful speculative builds already scheduled. This intervention reportedly lifts throughput from about 160 to around 250 lands per hour or more. Its explicit cost is that some interacting combinations are no longer tested together before merging.

The resulting architecture deliberately separates raw main from verified main. A post-merge system validates ranges of newly landed commits and advances the verified pointer only when the checked state passes. If validation fails, verified main remains at the last known-good commit while on-call prepares a fix or revert and sends it through the merge queue. Subsequent validation determines when the pointer can advance again. The speakers ultimately report peak throughput of roughly 300 lands per hour with P95 landing time restored to 30 minutes. Planned improvements include batching related changes to reduce builds, tracking green status per service or project rather than only repository-wide, and automating recovery. The lesson is a hybrid validation boundary: retain pre-merge checks where risk warrants them, move other integration validation after landing, and expose the verified state to consumers rather than pretending raw trunk is always healthy.

videos.title: AI Engineer NYC 2026 Closing Remarks - Ksenia Se, Turing Post & swyx, AI Engineer
videos.overview: Ksenia Se and swyx close AI Engineer NYC by emphasizing follow-through on new technical interests and professional relationships. They also discuss New York's AI community and announce upcoming coding-focused, European, and World's Fair events.
key_points: Ksenia summarizes the conference's breadth across agents, financial institutions, and world simulation, presenting new questions and investigation topics as a useful outcome.
swyx emphasizes New York's contributions to AI through financial institutions, research, infrastructure, and founders, and describes building a lasting local home for the community.

The announced event lineup includes the coding-focused Code summit, a second AI Engineer Europe in London in February, and a San Francisco World's Fair planned for the following summer with an announced scale of 10,000 people.
Both speakers emphasize continuing conversations after the conference; swyx also recommends Ksenia's Turing Post video work.
summary: Ksenia Se closes the three-day program by reflecting on its breadth, from agent development to applications in financial institutions and world simulation. Rather than attempting a technical recap, she suggests that attendees leaving with more subjects to investigate is an appropriate outcome for an engineering conference. She thanks the speakers, organizers, production crew, sponsors, partners, and participants who shared work and asked questions. Her forward-looking hope is that conversations begun at the event develop into projects or results that can be shared at a future AI Engineer gathering.

swyx then thanks Ksenia for returning as an MC and recommends her Turing Post videos, specifically recognizing the editing effort behind them. He describes the organizers' intention to establish a stronger, continuing presence in New York. His rationale is that the city's AI contribution deserves more recognition: he points to work inside financial institutions as well as research, infrastructure, and local founders. The remarks frame the conference as support for an existing technical community rather than only a temporary gathering of visiting speakers.

The closing announcements describe Code as the organization's first vertical summit and connect its focus on coding agents to swyx's view that coding is a leading area for verifiable AI. He also announces a second AI Engineer Europe in London in February and promotes a larger World's Fair in San Francisco for the following summer, describing an intended scale of 10,000 people. He finishes by encouraging attendees to maintain professional contacts and arrange their own meetings after returning home. The practical takeaway is continued community participation, not a new technical method or implementation prescription.
